newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals-Aluminium premiums cling to high perch.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals-Aluminium premiums cling to high perch.

text.p: Asian aluminium premiums remain strong on the back of brisk demand although upcoming talks on third quarter supply contracts may keep regional business quiet, metal dealers said on Friday.
"Aluminium demand around the region is quite good, especially from Southeast Asia," a dealer for a European metal trading company told Reuters.
"But the interesting time will be next month when negotiations on third quarter contracts are concluded in Japan, Korea and Taiwan," another European dealer said.

Premiums in Japan were seen at US$90-$95 a tonne CIF over LME cash prices against $85-$92 last week. They were quoted unchanged at $90-$95 a tonne CIF Jakarta, $90-$95 a tonne CIF Kaohsiung and Keelung and $90-$95 a tonne CIF Korean ports.
"The premiums are still holding very firmly," a dealer said, adding robust demand from the car and construction sectors were keeping them at fairly good levels.
LME aluminium stocks have been falling sharply because of good demand. Inventories dropped to 797,450 tonnes on Thursday, down more than 42,000 tonnes from the level about three weeks ago.
The only possible hindrance for consumers would be if LME aluminium prices climbed higher.

LME aluminium climbed as high as $1,647 a tonne on Wednesday before shedding gains and ending on Thursday $17 down on the day at $1,628. Three-month aluminium was quoted by the trade at 0400 GMT at $1,628/32 a tonne.
"We expect prices to remain in the $1,600-$1,650 range for now. Next resistance is seen at $1,660," LME brokers Brandeis said in its daily review.

"The higher prices go, the thinner the air becomes. An increase in LME prices may keep consumers quiet," a dealer said. In copper, Far East dealers said there was some concern about the strikes afflicting the Escondida and Quebrada Blanca copper mines in Chile.
"People are a bit nervous, but they're just talking about it so far. Unless we get further news, we won't see much impact in the market," a dealer said.

Some 350 of the 2,000 workers in Escondida, the world's biggest copper mine, have been on strike for about a week. On Wednesday, workers at Quebrada Blanca mine also walked out after rejecting a pay offer.
Escondida is owned by Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ-CRA. Quebrada Blanca is controlled by Cominco Ltd.

Traders said the market was also watching whether China, which was said to have taken out up to 8,000 tonnes of copper from the LME's Singapore warehouse, will ship the material back to the city-state.
Trading for the red metal was thin in Asia, with three month copper seen by dealers at 0400 GMT at $2,361/66 a tonne against the late London quote on Thursday of $2,364/67 a tonne.
Rumours also swirled around the market that China would ship about 5,000 tonnes of zinc to Singapore.
"There are rumours that Chinese zinc is on the way here," one dealer said.
"I heard those rumours last week, but I haven't seen them this week," a dealer for a Japanese trading house said.
